cards.explanation: The answer is embalm him. Joseph, Jacob's son, directs the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel, and they do it (Genesis 50:2). He gives the job to the people who work for him. The next verse says the embalming takes forty days to complete (Genesis 50:3). I think that tells us how carefully Joseph wanted his father looked after.

The answer is True. The verse says, “And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.” (Genesis 50:3). They mourn for Jacob, Joseph's father, and the text gives the number: seventy days. That's a long stretch on any calendar, friends.

The answer is that Jacob made Joseph swear to bury him in the land of Canaan. Joseph speaks to Pharaoh's court and asks them to pass his words to Pharaoh, Egypt's king (Genesis 50:4). In his message he says his father made him swear an oath when he said, “I am about to die. You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 50:5). So the oath is about Canaan, and about a tomb Jacob says he dug himself.
The answer is True. Joseph says, “Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.” (Genesis 50:5). In one breath he asks to go and tells them he'll come back. Short message, clear plan, friends.

The answer is, “Go up and bury your father.” Pharaoh says, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” (Genesis 50:6). That's a quick, clear yes, and it points right back to the oath. Joseph asked carefully and got a plain answer.

The answer is False, and you can count heads to see it. Joseph goes “…along with all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household.” (Genesis 50:8). Only their children and flocks and herds stay in Goshen. It's the biggest family trip I've ever heard of, and I once crowded six cookie cutters onto one counter.

The answer is that they lament and wail loudly. At the threshing floor of Atad, “…they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days.” (Genesis 50:10). That's grief you can hear from a distance. The next verse says the Canaanites living there see the mourning (Genesis 50:11).

The answer is the Egyptians. The Canaanites see the mourning and say, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). With that many chariots and Egyptian elders in the crowd, I can see how they'd say it. That's why the place across the Jordan got its name, Abel-mizraim.

The answer is Machpelah. Jacob's sons buried him “…in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre…” (Genesis 50:13). Abraham bought that field from Ephron the Hittite to use as a burial site. Joseph kept his oath, and the sons did as their father had charged them (Genesis 50:12).

The answer is that they're afraid Joseph will repay them for the evil they did. They say, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” (Genesis 50:15). Their father is gone, and they start imagining the worst. I think a guilty conscience can talk louder than anybody in the room.

The answer is forgive. The brothers say their father commanded, “I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.” (Genesis 50:17). That's an honest thing to say out loud. They name the wrong and ask for forgiveness anyway.
The answer is False. “When their message came to him, Joseph wept.” (Genesis 50:17). The text shows tears and no anger. After that, the brothers come to him themselves (Genesis 50:18).

The answer is that they say they are his slaves. The brothers come, bow down before Joseph, and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). They go all the way down and don't hold anything back. It's a big thing to say to your own brother.

The answer is “Do not be afraid.” That's Joseph's first word to them (Genesis 50:19). The brothers walked in scared, bowing low, and that's the first thing they hear. It's a kind way to start, friends.

The answer is good. Joseph says, “…what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good…” (Genesis 50:20). He doesn't pretend the evil didn't happen. He says God was working for good through it.

The answer is to preserve the lives of many people. Joseph tells his brothers that “…God intended for good…” what they meant for evil, and he names the purpose: “…to preserve the lives of many people.” (Genesis 50:20). Joseph points to lives kept safe. That's what he says a day like this was for.

The answer is True, and Joseph says it plainly. He tells them, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). The brothers came expecting trouble. What they get is a promise to look after them and their families.

The answer is True. The verse says, “He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation…” (Genesis 50:23). Ephraim is Joseph's son (Genesis 41:52). Joseph lives long enough to see great-grandchildren, and that's a full house, friends.

The answer is that God will bring them up to the land He promised. Joseph tells his brothers, “…God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath…” (Genesis 50:24). He's about to die, and he's still looking ahead. He trusts what God said He'd do.

The answer is that they must carry his bones up from Egypt. Joseph says, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” (Genesis 50:25). He wants his bones to go with them when God brings them up. Joseph trusted that day would come.

The answer is False. Joseph died at 110, and they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt (Genesis 50:26). The oath said his bones would be carried up after God attends to them (Genesis 50:25). I think this is a quiet moment, and it's fine to let it be.
